claims.text: Homogenization can produce a nominally single-phase FCC compositionally complex alloy.
The initial alloy can have minimal precipitates and grain-boundary segregation.
Localized short-range chemical ordering at or near grain boundaries can lower grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Brittle grain-boundary behavior can emerge in a compositionally complex solid solution without large-scale second-phase precipitation.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates promote dynamic short-range ordering near grain boundaries.
Short-range ordering near grain boundaries raises localized stress concentrations.
Short-range-order-induced weakening triggers intergranular or cleavage-like fracture.
Conventional single-phase alloys with simpler compositions do not typically develop comparably extensive ordering that promotes brittle boundary failure.
The as-homogenized compositionally complex alloy has high ductility and toughness.
The onset of short-range ordering near grain boundaries will correlate with a decrease in fracture toughness.
The onset of short-range ordering near grain boundaries will increase the propensity for boundary cracking.
Conventional single-phase controls of similar grain size and without strong short-range order will undergo milder toughness degradation under the same conditions.
Impurity segregation and hydrogen absorption can weaken grain boundaries and promote crack initiation in conventional metals and alloys.
Grain-boundary second-phase precipitation can cause stress and strain concentrations because particle and matrix deformation are incompatible.
Grain-boundary precipitation and coarse-particle formation are the primary conventional routes to toughness loss.
Above a critical temperature, diffusion substantially mitigates short-range-order effects.
Mitigation of short-range order at higher temperature restores higher ductility.
Very low strain rates diminish short-range-order-mediated grain-boundary brittleness.
Significantly higher temperatures diminish short-range-order-mediated grain-boundary brittleness.
Hydrogen exposure is a potential confounder in tests of grain-boundary embrittlement.
